chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-Amraki ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), said:
I asked him about the speckled crow and the black one — is it permissible to eat them both? So he said: 'It is not permissible to eat anything from the crows — neither the rook nor any other.'

key_terms.الْغُرَابُ الْأَبْقَعُ: The speckled/piebald crow — a crow with patches of black and white
key_terms.الْغِرْبَانُ: Plural of ghurāb (crow/raven) — encompassing all members of the crow family (Corvidae)
key_terms.زَاغٌ: A specific type of crow, often translated as rook or jackdaw
key_terms.يَحِلُّ: Is permissible/lawful (halal) — the standard jurisprudential term for lawfulness in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat crows in Shia Islam according to Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Ali ibn Ja'far reports that he asked Imam Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the permissibility of eating two types of crow: the speckled (al-abqa') and the all-black. The Imam issued a comprehensive ruling declaring that eating any type of crow — including the rook (zaghh) and all others — is forbidden (haram). This hadith reflects the classical Islamic jurisprudential tradition of categorizing birds as forbidden when they are carrion-eaters or have talons, and the Imam's answer extended the prohibition to the entire crow family without exception.
